task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bereft. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bereft should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: With both children settled overseas, the holidays left the couple feeling bereft, the table too big and the house too quiet.
Lacking is far milder than bereft — a report can be lacking in detail without anyone grieving over it.
Deprived is weaker than bereft — it notes that something was withheld or taken, without the aching sense of loss that bereft carries.

Devoid means simply empty of something, with no feeling of loss attached — a room devoid of furniture never misses it. Bereft is emptiness that grieves: the felt absence of a thing once possessed and now gone. Devoid states the emptiness; bereft mourns it.

Robbed means something was taken from you outright, and the word points at the crime and the taker. Bereft keeps only the loss itself: the mourned absence of what you once had, whether or not anyone took it. A burgled shop is robbed; a widowed heart is bereft.

The robber verb inside bereft — Old English reafian, 'to plunder' — dropped out of everyday English centuries ago, so there is no common cousin left to find. Only its own siblings survive: bereave, and bereaved for those the robbery of death has visited.
Bereft means devoid of, without.

The village lost its bus route in the spring cuts, and by autumn people spoke of being bereft of far more than transport: the 7:40 had been where engagements were announced, gossip settled, and quarrels patched up.
Bereft is sharper than plain 'without' because it carries the ache of having once had the thing.
It is the old past form of 'bereave' — to be bereft is literally to have been robbed, and the word keeps that sense of felt, personal loss.
Bereft is for the felt absence of something once possessed — bereft of hope, of company, of purpose — and it usually keeps its preposition: bereft of.
Plain 'without' states a fact; bereft mourns it.
Beside its unit-mates: forlorn looks abandoned and abject is degraded, but bereft always points at the particular treasure that is gone.

When the nightly radio serial 'Harbor Light' ended after forty-one years, the station braced for anger.
What arrived instead was grief.
Letters poured in from listeners who described themselves as bereft, and the word repaid attention.
Few complained about scheduling.
They wrote about a voice that had shared their kitchens each evening since childhood, now simply gone.
One farmer wrote that at eight o'clock his kitchen 'still leans toward the radio, and nothing arrives.' The station had expected to defend a business decision.
It found itself answering condolence letters, as after a death in ten thousand families.
